title: The Strange Story of the 1904 Olympic Marathon
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the 1904 Olympic marathon held in Saint Louis during the World's Fair (Louisiana Purchase Centennial Exhibition), widely considered the hardest marathon ever run. Topics include the origins of the marathon event in the 1896 Athens Games (proposed by Michel Bréal), James E. Sullivan's poor course design, purposeful dehydration theory, the dusty dirt-road course, the runners' misadventures (Fred Lorz's car ride and fake win, Felix Carvajal's nap and apple/peach snacking, Thomas Hicks' strychnine and brandy and eventual win, Billy Garcia's near-fatal injury, Sam Mellor's dropout), the South African runners Len Tau and Jan Mashiani, the Anthropology Games at the fair, and the 26.2-mile marathon distance lore. Ends with a listener mail item from Kathy about calling home to ask for the dog.

segments.title: Opening and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a listener suggestion from Peter Fitzgibbon about the 1904 Olympic marathon, described as the hardest marathon ever run.

segments.title: Origins of the Olympic marathon
segments.summary: Michel Bréal proposed a marathon race commemorating the Battle of Marathon and Pheidippides; the IOC added it to the 1896 Athens Games, where Greek runners took the top three spots, with Spyridon Louis the winner.

segments.title: 1904 Saint Louis Games context
segments.summary: The 1904 Games were the third Olympics and first in the US, overshadowed by the World's Fair; first games with gold, silver and bronze medals. George Eyser, a gymnast with a wooden leg, won six medals.

segments.title: James E. Sullivan and racism in early Olympics
segments.summary: James E. Sullivan, who organized the 1904 Games and ran American amateur sports, was described as xenophobic and racist; he pushed for Jim Thorpe's medals to be stripped, and refused women's and Black athletes' participation.

segments.title: Anthropology Games and human zoos
segments.summary: Sullivan, head of physical culture for the World's Fair, organized the Anthropology Games (called Special Olympics) pitting white Americans against indigenous people, who were not told the rules and lost lopsidedly.

segments.title: Course design, purposeful dehydration and heat
segments.summary: Sullivan designed the marathon using purposeful dehydration theory, with one water station near the twelve mile mark and disqualification for other drinking. It started at 3 p.m. in August heat around 90 degrees, on dirt roads with horses and cars kicking up dust, and included seven hills of 100 to 300 feet.

segments.title: Runners introduced
segments.summary: Thirty-two runners started and fourteen finished, the fewest finishers in Olympic history. Fred Lorz was a bricklayer who had won a five-mile race; Albert Corey worked at a Chicago slaughterhouse; Felix Carvajal from Cuba was a famous walker.

segments.title: Felix Carvajal's story
segments.summary: Carvajal, a 5'1" Cuban walker known as Andarín the Walker, had walked Cuba, hitchhiked to Saint Louis after Cuba would not pay his way, and arrived having not eaten for two days; he spoke a slangy Cuban dialect.

segments.title: South African runners Tau and Mashiani
segments.summary: Two Tswana men from South Africa, Len Tau and Jan Mashiani, were at the fair reenacting the Boer War and were brought in to add internationality to the race; they became the first Black African Olympians, and Tau was a mailman.

segments.title: Early dropouts and the dust
segments.summary: John Lordon vomited and quit before leaving the stadium; the dusty dirt roads choked runners. Fred Lorz quit at about mile ten and hitched a ride in a car.

segments.title: Carvajal's nap and Sam Mellor's dropout
segments.summary: Carvajal stopped to eat apples or peaches, got stomach cramps, and napped on the course. Sam Mellor, a favorite, cramped from dehydration around mile sixteen and dropped out. Billy Garcia coughed blood and needed emergency surgery.

segments.title: Thomas Hicks, strychnine and the cheating Fred Lorz
segments.summary: Thomas Hicks, a professional clown, was given egg whites, strychnine and brandy during the race. Fred Lorz was disqualified after a spectator revealed he had ridden in a car; Hicks was then first in line and was helped across the finish.

segments.title: Hicks finish and the Saint Louis report
segments.summary: Hicks was hallucinating near the end, carried across the finish by trainers, and finished in 3 hours 28 minutes, the slowest Olympic marathon gold; a Saint Louis newspaper described his condition.

segments.title: Aftermath, Sullivan's book, and the 26.2-mile distance
segments.summary: Only fourteen of thirty-two finished, a record dropout rate. Sullivan later wrote that drinking during marathons was not beneficial. The 1908 London Marathon set the 26.2-mile distance, supposedly due to the royal viewing box, though the hosts doubt the lore.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kathy and calling the dog
segments.summary: Kathy recounts calling home and asking for the family dog as a signal that they arrived safely, avoiding long-distance charges.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the show's production credit and listener contact information.
